priority: Decode toward 100 ms/token and 10 token/s without MTP

source.analysis_subject: bench: reject Decode GDN transient register state

global_loads.ncu_rule: 31.8 of 32 bytes per sector are used, and the observation applies to the 98.4 percent of sectors that miss L2

global_stores.interpretation: The sparse output/epilogue stores are only 0.366 percent of load-sector bytes and generate no measured L2 write lookup miss. The NCU store-pattern rule is therefore not a whole-kernel 49.93-percent opportunity.

decision.reason: The current down global loads already use 99.520 percent of each sector and L2-miss bytes are within 0.114 percent of the mandatory packed-weight plus scale6 payload. Removing every remaining measured load-sector inefficiency projects to only 0.093974 ms/token. Even adding an impossible perfect elimination of all store-sector waste reaches only 0.157985 ms/token, below the frozen 0.30-ms/token admission gate.
rejected_mechanisms: wavefront-major or K512-major preswizzle whose only benefit is better global coalescing
cross-core movement reduction based only on repacking the existing down byte stream
a 2.20-GiB full down sidecar without an independently demonstrated instruction-level mechanism
decision.reopen_when: Only a materially different mechanism that removes payload bytes or demonstrates an instruction/synchronization saving independent of coalescing, with a credible at-least-0.30-ms/token whole-Decode contribution.

claim_limits: This is a measured traffic-ceiling rejection, not an implemented candidate or achieved performance result.
The 0.093974-ms/token value linearly applies NCU's local load-pattern estimate to the current 20.192096-ms down stage; it is a screening ceiling, not a directly timed whole-model delta.
The 0.157985-ms/token combined value additionally assumes every unused load and store sector byte can be removed at zero cost, so it is deliberately optimistic.
The result rejects layout changes whose only mechanism is global transaction efficiency. It does not reject a future byte-removing representation or a separately proven instruction/dependency change.
MTP is outside this analysis and remains outside the current target path.
